citation: Giles v Thompson [1994] 1 AC 142 (HL)
title: Giles v Thompson; Devlin v Baslington
principle: The House of Lords (Lord Mustill) held that credit hire arrangements, under which a hire company supplies a replacement car on credit and pursues the charges against the at-fault driver, are not champertous or contrary to public policy, and that the hire charges are recoverable as damages for loss of use. CCGUK relies on it as the foundation of recoverability whenever an insurer attacks the credit hire arrangement itself rather than need, period or rate.

No BAILII URL for the 1993 HL judgment surfaced, so none is recorded; a human should locate it on BAILII (UKHL 1993) before citing a link.

citation: Dimond v Lovell [2000] UKHL 27; [2002] 1 AC 384
title: Dimond v Lovell
principle: A credit hire agreement that is a regulated consumer credit agreement but is improperly executed (missing prescribed terms) is unenforceable against the hirer under the Consumer Credit Act 1974, so the hirer has suffered no loss and recovers nothing; the hire company has no unjust enrichment claim either. The House also held that a claimant who could have hired without credit recovers only the basic (spot) hire rate, not the extra benefits bundled into credit hire. CCGUK uses it as the reason the hire agreement must be exempt (RAO art 60F) or fully compliant, and as the baseline that the full rate depends on impecuniosity.

[2002] 1 AC 384 report cite from the blueprint, not seen.

citation: Clark v Tull (t/a Ardington Electrical Services); Burdis v Livsey; Lagden v O'Connor and others [2002] EWCA Civ 510; [2003] QB 36
title: Burdis v Livsey (conjoined with Clark v Ardington Electrical Services)
principle: Conjoined Court of Appeal test cases on credit hire and credit repair after Dimond: agreements drafted to fall within the Consumer Credit Act exemption were held enforceable, the reasonable cost of repair is recoverable as the measure of the diminution in value whoever actually funded the repair, and an impecunious claimant may recover the credit hire rate (later affirmed in Lagden v O'Connor). CCGUK uses it for credit-repair recoverability and exemption drafting; 'Clark v Ardington' and 'Burdis v Livsey' are the same judgment.

citation: Lagden v O'Connor [2003] UKHL 64; [2004] 1 AC 1067
title: Lagden v O'Connor
principle: An impecunious claimant, meaning one who cannot pay spot-rate hire charges without making sacrifices he could not reasonably be expected to make, recovers the full credit hire charges because credit hire was his only realistic way of mitigating the loss of use caused by the defendant. This is the gateway to full-rate recovery; CCGUK must evidence impecuniosity (statement of means, bank statements, available credit) from sign-up rather than assert it.

citation: Bee v Jenson [2007] EWCA Civ 923; [2007] 4 All ER 791 (first instance [2006] EWHC 3359 (Comm))
title: Bee v Jenson
principle: A claimant whose replacement car was supplied under his own motor/legal-expenses insurance arrangements (DAS/Helphire) still recovers the reasonable cost of hire from the tortfeasor; a claimant's insurance arrangements are irrelevant to the defendant's liability (Bradburn principle). CCGUK uses it to answer the 'claimant paid nothing / car was insurer-provided' defence; recovery is of the reasonable hire cost, so rate evidence still matters.

citation: Copley v Lawn; Maden v Haller [2009] EWCA Civ 580; [2010] 1 All ER (Comm) 890
title: Copley v Lawn (with Maden v Haller)
principle: A claimant who declines or ignores the at-fault insurer's offer of a 'free' replacement car is not automatically in breach of the duty to mitigate: the offer must make its terms and cost clear enough for the claimant to evaluate it, and even where refusal is unreasonable the claimant still recovers what the car would have cost the insurer, not nil. CCGUK must log every intervention offer, reply in writing with reasons within one working day, and expect the insurer to argue that damages are capped at its own cost.

verification.sourceNote: Not fetched (egress proxy). Search-engine listing of the BAILII page 'Copley v Lawn & Ors [2009] EWCA Civ 580 (17 June 2009)' confirmed the citation; snippet confirmed the two cases (Copley: Helphire £39.90/day, KGM offer same day; Maden: KGM offer within 24 hours ignored, Helphire £156.80/day) and the court's scepticism that a claimant must take further mitigation steps beyond not hiring above market rate.

citation: Beechwood Birmingham Ltd v Hoyer Group UK Ltd [2010] EWCA Civ 647; [2011] QB 357
title: Beechwood Birmingham Ltd v Hoyer Group UK Ltd
principle: Where a business with a pool of vehicles loses the use of one that was not revenue-earning and had spare capacity, loss of use is compensated by general damages measured by interest on the capital tied up and depreciation over the repair period, not by a notional hire rate; Lord Scott's hire-rate dictum in Lagden is confined to private motorists who actually hire. CCGUK uses it for fleet and business loss-of-use claims: hire is only recoverable if the business genuinely had no spare vehicle, otherwise claim interest-and-depreciation damages.

Blueprint gloss ('a business with a spare fleet still recovers loss-of-use damages') is consistent. URL follows the BAILII pattern; not displayed in results.

citation: W v Veolia Environmental Services (UK) plc [2011] EWHC 2020 (QB); [2012] 1 All ER (Comm) 667
title: W v Veolia Environmental Services (UK) plc
principle: A credit hire agreement signed at the claimant's home when the car was delivered, without the written notice of cancellation rights required by the Cancellation of Contracts made in a Consumer's Home or Place of Work etc. Regulations 2008 (reg 7), was unenforceable against the hirer, so the hire charges were not a recoverable loss. The 2008 Regulations have been replaced by the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, whose mechanism differs (extended cancellation period and no liability for services supplied without the required information or an express request), but the commercial lesson is identical: CCGUK must give the Schedule 2 information, the Schedule 3 form and obtain an express request to start.

citation: Pattni v First Leicester Buses Ltd; Bent v Highways and Utilities Construction Ltd [2011] EWCA Civ 1384; [2012] RTR 17; [2012] Lloyd's Rep IR 577
title: Pattni v First Leicester Buses Ltd; Bent v Highways and Utilities Construction Ltd (No 2)
principle: In one conjoined judgment (Aikens LJ, 24 November 2011) the Court of Appeal set out how a judge should find the basic hire rate: identify what the claimant would reasonably have paid to hire a comparable vehicle in the locality for the period actually needed, using the best available evidence of mainstream rates, and make a reasoned assessment rather than reject imperfect evidence; the credit element is stripped out and the rate should reflect the actual length of hire. Paragraph 73 also addresses loss-of-use claims. CCGUK uses it to structure its own contemporaneous rate evidence (vehicle class, locality, date, period) and to attack insurers' spot-rate exhibits built from unrepresentative quotes.

citation: Sayce v TNT (UK) Ltd [2011] EWCA Civ 1583; [2012] 1 WLR 1261
title: Sayce v TNT (UK) Ltd
principle: Where a claimant unreasonably refused the defendant's offer of a free replacement car and instead hired on credit, the Court of Appeal held itself bound by Copley v Lawn: damages are the cost the defendant would have incurred in providing the car (agreed at £14 a day, £868 in total), not nil; the court declined TNT's invitation to depart from Copley. CCGUK uses it with Copley on intervention offers. CORRECTION: the blueprint's gloss ('unenforceable hire agreement means no recoverable hire loss') describes a different line of authority (Dimond, W v Veolia, Salat v Barutis); Sayce is a mitigation/intervention-offer case.

citation: Opoku v Tintas [2013] EWCA Civ 1299
title: Opoku v Tintas
principle: An impecunious claimant must still mitigate: the Court of Appeal upheld a finding that, after a reasonable time, Mr Opoku (hire of some £130,000 and £19,600 recovery and storage after a rear-end shunt) should have funded the repair himself by saving modest sums and using his credit-card facility, so hire and storage were cut off at that point; a claimant's available credit facilities are relevant to what he can reasonably be expected to fund. CCGUK uses it on period: impecuniosity justifies the rate but not an open-ended hire where the client could have got the car repaired sooner. CORRECTION: the blueprint attributed to this case the principle that failing to respond to an insurer's offer is a failure to mitigate; that is Copley v Lawn / Sayce v TNT, not Opoku.

citation: Coles v Hetherton [2013] EWCA Civ 1704; [2015] 1 WLR 160
title: Coles and others v Hetherton and others
principle: Physical damage to a vehicle is itself the loss; the measure is the diminution in value, which is normally represented by the reasonable cost of repair assessed objectively, and the claimant can recover that reasonable cost even where his own insurer arranged and paid for the repairs under its own commercial arrangements. CCGUK uses it as the basis for engineer-approved repair estimates and to resist insurers' attempts to limit repair recovery to what a subrogated insurer actually paid.

citation: Stevens v Equity Syndicate Management Ltd [2015] EWCA Civ 93; [2015] 4 WLR 24
title: Stevens v Equity Syndicate Management Ltd
principle: Kitchin LJ held that the basic hire rate is the lowest reasonable rate quoted by a mainstream supplier (or, if none, a local reputable supplier) for the kind of vehicle actually hired, in the claimant's locality at the time; the judge should identify that rate rather than average the quotes, and the difference from the credit hire charge represents the irrecoverable benefits that are stripped out. CCGUK should price its files on the assumption that a non-impecunious client recovers only the lowest reasonable mainstream rate, and should collect its own dated local quotes.

citation: McBride v UK Insurance Ltd; Clayton v EUI Ltd [2017] EWCA Civ 144; [2017] RTR 27
title: McBride v UK Insurance Ltd (with Clayton v EUI Ltd)
principle: Conjoined appeals refining Stevens: where the comparable basic hire rate quotes carry an excess, the court may add the reasonable cost of a stand-alone excess-elimination product to arrive at the recoverable rate for a nil-excess credit hire, and where only 7-day rates are available for a longer hire the judge may reasonably use them as the best evidence. CCGUK should treat the nil-excess element as a separate, evidenced head (cost of excess cover) and obtain rate evidence matched to the actual hire length.

citation: Irving v Morgan Sindall plc [2018] EWHC 1147 (QB)
title: Irving v Morgan Sindall plc
principle: Turner J (15 May 2018) decided two questions: a claimant who remains contractually liable for credit hire charges suffers a real loss even if assured she will never have to pay out of her own pocket, so the 'no loss' defence fails; and impecuniosity does not require destitution: the test is whether the claimant could reasonably have afforded spot-rate hire without unreasonable sacrifice (here a Ford Ka written off, hire of over four months and £20,109.60 while awaiting the insurer's cheque). CCGUK uses it against 'she will never pay' arguments and to frame the impecuniosity threshold. CORRECTION: the blueprint's gloss ('BHR assessed on a common-sense basis from imperfect evidence') better describes Bunting v Zurich; Irving is about the no-loss defence and the impecuniosity threshold.

citation: Hussain v EUI Ltd [2019] EWHC 2647 (QB)
title: Hussain v EUI Ltd
principle: Pepperall J (10 October 2019) gave guidance on credit hire claims by self-employed taxi and private hire drivers: the ordinary measure of loss while the plated vehicle is off the road is the lost profit, and where the cost of hiring a replacement plated vehicle is about the same as the avoided lost profit the court will not count the pennies, but where hire significantly exceeds the lost profit damages are ordinarily limited to the lost profit unless the claimant proves a reasonable need for the vehicle for other purposes (such as private or family use). CCGUK must gather profit evidence and non-business need evidence for every PHV client before hiring a plated replacement. CORRECTION: the blueprint described this case as 'comparators for BHR evidence'; its real significance is the lost-profit measure for taxi drivers.

citation: Irani v Duchon [2019] EWCA Civ 1846
title: Irani v Duchon
principle: NOT A CREDIT HIRE AUTHORITY. This is a personal injury appeal (judgment 6 November 2019) about future loss of earnings: the Court of Appeal considered when a trial judge may make a lump-sum Blamire award and a Smith v Manchester award instead of a multiplier/multiplicand calculation, after a 2013 road accident in which liability was not in issue and damages of £406,688 were awarded. It says nothing about basic hire rates or comparator vehicle classes and must not be cited for them; CCGUK refers injury claims out in any event.

citation: Diriye v Bojaj [2020] EWCA Civ 1400; [2021] 1 WLR 1277
title: Diriye v Bojaj and another
principle: A claimant who relies on impecuniosity to justify credit hire rates must plead it properly and prove it with disclosure (wage slips, bank and credit-card statements); a bare assertion in the particulars is not enough, and failure to comply with an unless order to particularise and disclose can debar the claimant from relying on impecuniosity at all (relief from sanctions was refused). The appeal also settled that CPR 6.26 deemed service applies to documents other than the claim form. CCGUK collects the statement of means and three months of statements at sign-up so the impecuniosity case is ready before any defence is served.

citation: Mattocks v Mann [1993] RTR 13 (CA)
title: Mattocks v Mann
principle: The Court of Appeal held that the reasonable hire period was not cut short because repairs were delayed while the claimant waited for her insurers to pay the repairer: in modern conditions substantial repair bills are expected to be funded by insurers, and absent a supervening event or a specific failure to mitigate by the claimant (or someone for whom she is responsible) the delay remains the tortfeasor's responsibility. CCGUK uses it on period disputes: keep a dated chronology and require the insurer to identify a specific failure to mitigate rather than merely pointing at the length of hire.

citation: Darbishire v Warran [1963] 1 WLR 1067; [1963] EWCA Civ 2 (CA)
title: Darbishire v Warran
principle: Where the cost of repairing a damaged vehicle greatly exceeds its market value, a claimant who repairs it anyway fails to mitigate and recovers only the pre-accident market value (credit being given for sums received) plus reasonable hire while a replacement is sourced; the 1951 Lea-Francis was repaired for £192 against a market value of about £85. This is the uneconomic-repair rule that underpins CCGUK's total-loss assessment and PAV engine: the ceiling on a repair claim is the cost of an equivalent replacement.

citation: Zurich Insurance plc v Umerji [2014] EWCA Civ 357
title: Zurich Insurance plc v Umerji
principle: Underhill LJ (25 March 2014) held that reasonableness of hire is assessed by need, rate and duration, and that a claimant who relies on impecuniosity must plead and prove it (para 37); a claimant debarred from relying on impecuniosity after failing to give disclosure must be treated as able to fund a replacement for his written-off car, so a 591-day hire costing about £95,130 was cut to a reasonable period after he knew it was a write-off. On rate, because the insurer adduced no basic hire rate evidence the credit hire rate was recoverable for the allowed period. CCGUK uses it both ways: prove impecuniosity properly, and hold insurers to their burden of producing BHR evidence.

citation: Kindertons Ltd v Murtagh and esure Services Ltd [2024] EWHC 471 (KB)
title: Kindertons Ltd v Murtagh and another
principle: Turner J (5 March 2024) upheld a non-party costs order against a credit hire company after the claimant's personal injury and hire claim failed for fundamental dishonesty and she disappeared leaving the costs order unpaid: the company had funded the hire on deferred terms, exercised control over the litigation and stood to benefit from it, so it was just to make it pay the insurer's costs notwithstanding QOCS. CCGUK treats this as a direct costs exposure: weak or dishonest-risk files should not run on credit hire, and acceptance scoring must be strict.

citation: Tescher v Direct Accident Management Ltd; AXA Insurance UK plc v Spectra Drive Ltd [2025] EWCA Civ 733
title: Tescher v Direct Accident Management Ltd (with AXA Insurance UK plc v Spectra Drive Ltd)
principle: Birss LJ (with Nicola Davies and Coulson LJJ, 13 June 2025) allowed both insurers' appeals and set out a two-stage approach to non-party costs orders against credit hire companies when a QOCS-protected claim fails: first, is the jurisdiction engaged because, as a matter of practical and economic reality, the credit hire company was the real party or real beneficiary of the litigation (where hire charges dwarf the other heads, the litigation is for all practical purposes the hire company's); second, what order is just, including how costs are attributed between heads. A 100% order was made against DAML and a 65% order against Spectra was reinstated. CCGUK's acceptance engine measures the hire-to-other-heads ratio as a costs-exposure signal. CAUTION: a further appeal to the UK Supreme Court appears to have been lodged (UKSC 2025/0116); check its status before relying on the Court of Appeal's test.

citation: Motor Insurers' Bureau v Houston [2025] EWHC 3178 (KB)
title: Motor Insurers' Bureau v Houston
principle: Cavanagh J, on appeal from Recorder Brown in the County Court at Birmingham, dismissed the MIB's appeal: a case-management order that debarred the claimant from relying on impecuniosity 'for the purpose of the rate of hire' did not stop him relying on his limited means to justify the length of hire (197 days of a Mercedes GLA from Easidrive at £224.29 a day) or the storage charges, so the full period was recoverable. The scope of a debarring order turns on its precise wording, in contrast to Zurich v Umerji where the claimant was treated as pecunious for all purposes. CCGUK must read every debarring or unless order literally and comply with impecuniosity disclosure in full.

citation: Fairclough Homes Ltd v Summers [2012] UKSC 26; [2012] 1 WLR 2004
title: Summers v Fairclough Homes Ltd
principle: The Supreme Court held that a court has power (CPR 3.4(2)(b) and its inherent jurisdiction) to strike out a grossly and dishonestly exaggerated claim as an abuse of process even after trial, but that doing so where the claimant has a genuine entitlement will very rarely be proportionate; the usual response is costs, interest and contempt or criminal sanctions. Parliament later added the fundamental dishonesty dismissal power for personal injury claims (CJCA 2015 s.57). CCGUK uses it to explain to clients why any inflated head endangers the whole file and to justify the file-exit rule when an account is shown to be false.

citation: Singh v Yaqubi [2013] EWCA Civ 23; [2013] RTR 24
title: Singh v Yaqubi
principle: The Court of Appeal (29 January 2013) dismissed a claim for some £92,000 of credit hire of a replacement Rolls-Royce because the business partnership that owned the damaged car had not proved a genuine need for a replacement of that kind, stressing that credit hire claims must be carefully controlled through the doctrine of mitigation and that need is a matter of evidence, especially for a business with access to other vehicles. CCGUK's need gate requires a statement of need describing actual journeys and any other vehicles available before a prestige or any replacement is supplied.

citation: Salat v Barutis [2013] EWCA Civ 1499; [2014] RTR 10
title: Salat v Barutis
principle: A credit hire agreement for a replacement motorcycle signed at the claimant's home (BLD, 9 May 2009) without the cancellation notice required by the Cancellation of Contracts made in a Consumer's Home or Place of Work etc. Regulations 2008 was unenforceable against the hirer; the defendant tortfeasor was entitled to take the point, and the court had no discretion to enforce the agreement regardless, so the hire charges were not recoverable (following W v Veolia). Under the current Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 the consequence is different in form (extended cancellation period and no liability for services supplied without the required information or express request) but the lesson for CCGUK is the same: paperwork failures at the doorstep destroy the hire claim.

citation: Sobrany v UAB Transtira [2016] EWCA Civ 28; [2016] Lloyd's Rep IR 266
title: Sobrany v UAB Transtira
principle: The claimant's credit hire charges remained recoverable although he held legal-expenses/after-the-event insurance that would ultimately indemnify him; the Court of Appeal (28 January 2016) treated the insurance as irrelevant between claimant and tortfeasor and held that, where his liability for hire and legal costs exceeded the limit under each of two policies but not their combined limit, he was indemnified under both, so he was not left without a recoverable loss. CCGUK cites it alongside Bee v Jenson when an insurer argues that a client's own insurance or ATE arrangements mean no loss.

citation: Bunting v Zurich Insurance plc [2020] EWHC 1807 (QB)
title: Bunting v Zurich Insurance plc
principle: The High Court dismissed a claimant's appeal against an award at the lowest basic hire rate for a prestige replacement (credit hire of £28,551.84 after a June 2015 accident): the claimant was not impecunious, he was entitled to a comparable prestige car but only at the BHR, and his 'nit-picking' attacks on the insurer's rate evidence (a 30-day maximum hire term, no evidence of deposits, no specific availability evidence) failed because courts take a common-sense, broad-brush approach to imperfect rates evidence. CCGUK should expect insurers' BHR evidence to be accepted unless there is a substantive flaw, and should rely on impecuniosity, not evidential quibbles, for full-rate recovery.

citation: Holt v Allianz Insurance plc [2023] EWHC 790 (KB)
title: Holt v Allianz Insurance plc
principle: Andrew Baker J (4 April 2023) allowed the claimant's appeal against an order for pre-action disclosure of bank, credit-card and savings statements and wage slips sought by the at-fault insurer to test impecuniosity in a hire-only claim (RTA 16 July 2020, hire by Auxillis): the application failed under CPR 31.16(3)(b) because the insurer itself was unlikely to be a party to the eventual proceedings, which would be brought against the driver. The judgment nonetheless signals that such financial disclosure is otherwise within reach and that refusing to engage on impecuniosity pre-action carries risk. CCGUK should have the impecuniosity pack ready and decide deliberately whether to disclose it pre-action.

citation: Dickinson v Tesco plc [2013] EWCA Civ 36; [2013] RTR 27
title: Dickinson v Tesco plc (and three other test cases)
principle: Four test cases decided together (4 February 2013) after the Autofocus rates-evidence scandal: it is for the defendant to prove that the credit hire charge exceeds the basic hire rate, that is to prove the credit element that is to be stripped out under Dimond; where the only BHR evidence was tainted and withdrawn, the credit hire rate stood. CCGUK uses it to hold insurers to their burden on rate and to scrutinise the provenance of any rates report served against it.

citation: Ali v HSF Logistics Polska Sp. z o.o. [2024] EWCA Civ 1479
title: Majid Ali v HSF Logistics Polska Sp. z o.o.
principle: Stuart-Smith LJ (4 December 2024) held that the absence of a valid MOT certificate (expired four and a half months before the accident) neither broke the chain of causation nor justified refusing recovery on illegality grounds: the defendant's tort deprived the claimant of the use of his car, driving without an MOT is a low-level offence, and denying the claim would be disproportionate, so credit hire of £21,588.72 for 36 days was recoverable, reversing the High Court. CCGUK checks MOT, tax and insurance at intake because they affect need and credibility, but a lapsed MOT is not fatal to a hire claim.

citation: Armstead v Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Co Ltd [2024] UKSC 6; [2024] 2 WLR 632
title: Armstead v Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Company Ltd
principle: The Supreme Court (14 February 2024) held that a credit-hire customer who had possessory title to the hire car when it was damaged by the defendant's insured could recover the sum she was contractually liable to pay the hire company for its loss of use (clause 16: the daily rate up to 30 days, £1,560), because a contractual liability to a third party consequent on physical damage to property in the claimant's possession is not pure economic loss and is recoverable unless the defendant proves it was too remote or an unreasonable pre-estimate. CCGUK's own hire agreement should contain a reasonable, evidenced loss-of-use clause so that damage to a fleet car by a third party is recoverable in the same way.

citation: Accident Exchange Ltd v Broom and others [2017] EWHC 1096 (Admin)
title: Accident Exchange Ltd v Broom and others (Autofocus contempt)
principle: The Divisional Court (24 May 2017) found former Autofocus rates surveyors in contempt of court for giving false basic-hire-rate evidence in credit hire cases, confirming that fabricated or untraceable comparables are not merely weak evidence but criminal. CCGUK's rate evidence must therefore be captured manually with URL, screenshot, timestamp and hash, and any rates report served by an insurer should be tested for provenance.
